
### diversion: some queuing theory 


* queuing theory: applied probability
* talks about how queues work 
<hr class="vspace" />
* applies to networks and anything else with ‘‘waiting in line’’


### queue measurements  {.smaller}


* arrival rate
* service time (amount of time after waiting in line)
* utilization = arrival rate / service time 
<hr class="vspace" />
* if single thing can be processed at a time, then max utilization = 100% 

   * higher implies ‘‘infinitely’’ long queues



### M/M/1/$\infty$ queue  {.smaller}


* next slides: results for M/M/1/$\infty$ queue 
<hr class="vspace" />
* M (memoryless) --- random arrival (exponential dist.)
* M --- random service time (exponential dist.)
* 1 --- one ‘‘server’’ (thing that can process packets)
* $\infty$ --- unlimited queue length


### M/M/1/$\infty$ queue length  {.smaller}



* mean queue length \[\frac{\text{arrival rate}}{\text{service rate} - \text{arrival rate}}\]
 ![](/congest/texfig/diversion-queuing-theory-mm1infty-queue-length.figure.svg)
 

* practical implication: <em>need to run networks at much less than full utilization</em>


### M/M/1/$\infty$ queue length std. deviation 



* \[\sqrt{\frac{\text{utilization}}{\left(1 - \text{utilization}\right)^2}}\]
 ![](/congest/texfig/diversion-queuing-theory-mm1infty-queue-length-std-deviation.figure.svg)
